findings.headline: Usable capital reserves forecast to decline 84% over three years, from £30.8m to £5.1m
findings.detail: Capital receipts and grants will be depleted significantly over the 2026/27 to 2027/28 period due to committed capital spending, declining from £30.8m to £5.1m. Report notes that this projection excludes uncertainty around receipts from Dove Lane sale.
findings.matters: Sharp decline in capital funding capacity constrains ability to fund future capital without increased borrowing or reserves depletion; uncertainty about Dove Lane adds execution risk
findings.figures: Capital reserves: £30,766k (2025/26) declining to £5,065k (2027/28), 84% reduction
findings.quote: usable capital reserve balances dropping significantly over the period due to existing commitments

findings.headline: Council carries £26.3m of unfunded capital spend funded through internal borrowing against cash balances
findings.detail: The council has no external borrowing but holds a Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) of £26.3m related to previous unfunded capital investments (including Platinum Stages and loans to subsidiary companies). This is funded by drawing on internal cash balances rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Significant internal borrowing constrains future borrowing capacity and ties up cash reserves that could provide liquidity buffer; indicates previous capital decisions created ongoing funding gaps
findings.figures: £26,301k CFR, no external borrowing
findings.quote: a need to borrow of £26,301k (also known as the Capital Financing Requirement or CFR) which is in relation to previous unfunded capital spend, such as the Platinum Stages and loans to subsidiary and related companies

findings.headline: £2.9m planned development of Cannon Public House cancelled; property now held for sale
findings.detail: A capital investment of £2.9m in developing a public house property has been withdrawn. The council is now selling the asset rather than completing the development.
findings.matters: Signals a shift in council investment strategy; conversion of development asset to sale removes planned future capital release and suggests development challenges
findings.quote: £2,937k Cannon Public House: development no longer going ahead, now held for sale.

findings.headline: £15.9m capital spending deferred to future years, equal to 57% of this year's planned budget
findings.detail: Capital spend was £8.5m against revised budget of £28.2m, with £15.9m slippage to future years. Major deferrals include: Catterick Way £3.2m, CIL-funded projects £3.6m, parks projects £2.9m, Darkes Lane £2.3m (being rescoped), temporary accommodation £0.5m. Projects now concentrated in 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: Large-scale, sustained capital slippage suggests project delivery challenges; future years will face concentrated spending demands and potential funding pressure
findings.figures: £15,964k slippage, £28,214k revised budget, £3,243k Catterick Way, £3,641k CIL projects, £2,913k parks, £2,344k Darkes Lane
findings.quote: The year-end variance of £19,740k includes project slippage which will be re-profiled in the capital programme to future years totalling £15,964k, under spends amounting to £3,895k and an overspend of (£119k).

findings.headline: Rental income from key council assets fell £1.3m due to asbestos remediation and tenant departure
findings.detail: Asset Management shows £1,427k deficit. Elstree Film Studios rent was cut by £300k due to asbestos remediation; Platinum Stages lost £957k when a tenant used a break clause in July 2025. A new tenant was secured in June 2026, with recovery to budget level (£1.7m) expected for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Material loss of revenue income from commercial assets directly affects council's financial resilience and ability to invest in services
findings.figures: £1,427k deficit, £1,257k total shortfall, £300k from Studios, £957k from Platinum Stages
findings.quote: there was a loss of (£957k) from the Platinum Stages following the departure of the original tenant in July 2025, the tenant having initiated the three-year break clause in their agreement.

findings.paper_title: AppA-Red, new and changed risks June 2026-SRMS
findings.headline: Housing requirement increased to 1,034 dwellings per annum - infrastructure and service demand implications
findings.detail: New NPPF (December 2024) increased Hertsmere's housing target to 1,034 dwellings per annum from previous level. This creates immediate infrastructure investment needs and increased service demand (schools, social care, waste, transport). Combined with Special Measures Planning status limiting the council's negotiating power, this creates tension between growth mandates and the council's reduced ability to secure developer contributions.
findings.matters: Housing targets drive capital investment requirements and service demand proportional to growth. Special Measures status reduces the council's ability to condition development or secure S106 contributions to fund required supporting infrastructure.
findings.figures: 1,034 dwellings per annum (new NPPF December 2024 requirement)
findings.quote: New NPPF published in December 2024 – housing numbers have increased to 1034 per annum for Hertsmere.

findings.paper_title: AppA-Red, new and changed risks June 2026-SRMS
findings.headline: LGR (Local Government Reorganisation) - government decision imminent with material uncertainty about council's future structure
findings.detail: Three LGR models submitted to government November 2025; government decision expected summer 2026 (imminent at time of this review, dated 30/06/2026). Transition work commenced January 2026. Council acknowledges risk that outcome could 'not benefit Hertsmere residents, businesses and staff' with potential 'negative impact on service delivery'.
findings.matters: LGR could fundamentally alter council structure, operations, service delivery and financial position. Uncertainty during transition period creates risk to financial stability, planning certainty and serviceability.
findings.figures: Three models proposed; government decision timing: summer 2026; transition work commenced January 2026
findings.quote: the outcome may not benefit Hertsmere residents, businesses and staff negatively impacting on service delivery

findings.paper_title: AppA-Red, new and changed risks June 2026-SRMS
findings.headline: Loan exposure to Elstree Film Studios subsidiary with documented repayment risk
findings.detail: Council has lent to Elstree Film Studios (EFS), identified as a key subsidiary investment 'to generate ongoing revenue stream'. Risk register explicitly lists 'failure of EFS to repay loan' as a specific local risk under external financial pressures. Loan amount not disclosed.
findings.matters: Loan to subsidiary represents direct credit risk to the council. Default would eliminate expected revenue stream and write off capital, exacerbating the medium-term budget pressures and reserve position documented elsewhere.
findings.figures: Loan amount not specified; EFS one of three subsidiaries: Elstree Film Studios, Hertsmere Development Limited, Hertsmere Living Limited
findings.quote: failure of EFS to repay loan

findings.paper_title: AppA-Red, new and changed risks June 2026-SRMS
findings.headline: Medium-term budget pressures: balanced budget achievable only to 2028/9, structural issues unresolved beyond
findings.detail: Risk register states balanced budget 'can be set to 2028/9', indicating structural pressures beyond this horizon remain unresolved. Current mitigation relies on 'levels of reserves to help meet any budget shortfall in the short-term', implying ongoing reserve drawdowns and unplanned deficit.
findings.matters: Indicates structural deficit requiring either service reductions, further borrowing, or reserve depletion after 2028/9. Limits medium-term financial flexibility and borrowing capacity available to service additional debt.
findings.figures: Balanced budget only to 2028/9; beyond that horizon unplanned
findings.quote: Balanced budget can be set to 2028/9

findings.paper_title: AppA-Red, new and changed risks June 2026-SRMS
findings.headline: Special Measures Planning Authority designation limits planning income and discretion
findings.detail: Council formally designated as Special Measures Planning Authority due to high appeal overturn rates. This allows certain planning applications to bypass the council and go directly to Planning Inspectorate, resulting in loss of planning fee income and inability to negotiate Section 106 infrastructure contributions from developers.
findings.matters: Planning fees and S106 contributions are material sources of capital income for councils. Loss of discretion also removes the council's ability to condition development or secure infrastructure funding from developers for growth-related needs.
findings.figures: None quantified in document
findings.quote: As a result of a high percentage of planning decisions being overturned at appeal and the reduction in the threshold percentage the council has been designated by the Secretary of State due to poor performance in handling large scale planning applications.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Statement and Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26-SIAS
findings.headline: IT Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity audit received Limited Assurance, one of four limited audits in operational areas
findings.detail: The IT Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity audit was one of four audits to receive Limited Assurance status during 2025-26, with 1 High and 3 Medium priority recommendations. The council also received Limited Assurance for Garages, Mandatory Training, and Bank Reconciliations.
findings.matters: Limited assurance in disaster recovery indicates the council may struggle to restore critical systems and maintain financial controls following an IT incident. Lenders depend on councils' ability to sustain service continuity and financial operations under disruption.
findings.figures: 4 Limited Assurance audits (20% of 20 total); IT Disaster Recovery had 1 High and 3 Medium recommendations; 14 audit days allocated
findings.quote: During 2025/26, SIAS issued four limited assurance audit reports, these being audits of the systems related to aspects of Garages, Mandatory Training, IT Disaster Recovery and Bank Reconciliations.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Statement and Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26-SIAS
findings.headline: Eleven Medium-priority audit recommendations remain unimplemented at year-end, with longest overdue by 10 months
findings.detail: As of March 2026, 11 Medium-priority audit recommendations had not been implemented. The longest outstanding recommendation was 10 months overdue its agreed target date. Management provided revised target dates, but this indicates slow progress in remediating identified control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Outstanding recommendations indicate management is not prioritizing remediation of identified control weaknesses. A lender needs assurance that audit findings are actively being addressed. Slippage of 10 months suggests either inadequate resources or lack of urgency in fixing controls.
findings.figures: 11 Medium-priority outstanding; longest 10 months overdue; 74 total recommendations made in year
findings.quote: The longest outstanding recommendation was 10 months overdue. Progress in management completing agreed actions will continue to be monitored and reported to the Audit Committee within our progress reports

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Statement and Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26-SIAS
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation audit found grant payment incorrectly posted to balance sheet, resulting in Limited Assurance rating
findings.detail: The Financial Services Manager identified a grant payment that was incorrectly posted in the balance sheet, accounting for most of the reconciling difference. This control failure resulted in Limited Assurance status with 1 High and 3 Medium priority recommendations. Bank reconciliation is a fundamental control over accurate financial reporting.
findings.matters: Grant funding is material council revenue. Misposting grant payments to the balance sheet indicates a weakness in financial posting and reconciliation controls. Lenders need assurance that the council's financial statements accurately reflect transactions and grant receipts.
findings.figures: 1 High priority recommendation; 3 Medium recommendations; Limited Assurance status; 10 audit days allocated
findings.quote: Specifically, for bank reconciliations, the Financial Services Manager identified a grant payment that had been incorrectly posted in the balance sheet which accounted for most of the reconciling difference.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Statement and Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26-SIAS
findings.headline: Overall control opinion is Reasonable Assurance rather than Substantial, indicating material control gaps exist
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive concluded Reasonable Assurance on the council's control framework, meaning some issues and scope for improvement were identified that may put at risk the achievement of objectives. Only 1 of 20 assurance audits (5%) achieved Substantial Assurance; 13 achieved Reasonable (65%); 4 received Limited Assurance (20%).
findings.matters: Reasonable Assurance means the control environment is not best practice; there are known weaknesses. Lenders require confidence in financial and operational controls, and Reasonable Assurance indicates a lower level of control maturity than best practice requires.
findings.figures: 1 Substantial (5%), 13 Reasonable (65%), 4 Limited (20%), 2 Consultancy (10%)
findings.quote: Our overall opinion is Reasonable Assurance - There is a generally sound system of governance, risk management and control in place. Some issues, non-compliance or scope for improvement were identified which may put at risk the achievement of objectives in the area audited.

findings.headline: Bank Reconciliations flagged as significant governance issue
findings.detail: The council identifies Bank Reconciliations as a significant governance issue in the 2025/26 AGS Action Plan. Full details are provided in Appendix A of the report.
findings.matters: Formal identification of bank reconciliation issues indicates control weaknesses in basic financial management; these are fundamental controls that affect reporting accuracy.
findings.quote: This relates to the late publication of the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25, Bank Reconciliations, Planning and Appeals, and Cyber Security

findings.headline: 2024/25 Statement of Accounts published late
findings.detail: The council identifies late publication of the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25 as a significant governance issue in its 2025/26 AGS Action Plan. This indicates delays in the council's financial reporting and accounts closure process.
findings.matters: Delays in publishing audited accounts signal potential control or capacity issues in financial management; lenders use timely reporting as an indicator of council governance strength.
findings.quote: This relates to the late publication of the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25, Bank Reconciliations, Planning and Appeals, and Cyber Security

findings.headline: Full asset condition survey deferred in 2025 due to resource constraints, leaving maintenance liabilities unmeasured
findings.detail: The council did not complete a full portfolio-wide condition survey in 2025 because of 'resource constraints'. The last completed survey identified £1.8m of maintenance investment needed over 10 years and a further £1.1m required in years 11-30. A targeted assessment of roofs on seven retail parades identified £0.9m in highest priority work, but this is explicitly 'not expected to be sufficient to fund all works identified'. The council has recently appointed a part-time Building Surveyor to eventually release capacity for a wider condition survey, but this creates a visibility gap in known asset liabilities.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what maintenance and asset renewal obligations the council actually holds. Without a current condition survey, there is quantifiable uncertainty in the capital plan about whether maintenance spending is adequate or underestimated.
findings.figures: Last completed survey: £1.8m over 10 years (years 1-10), £1.1m (years 11-20), £0.3m (years 21-30). Current roof work budget: £0.9m, identified as insufficient.
findings.quote: due to resource constraints, a full portfolio-wide condition survey was not undertaken in 2025

findings.headline: Local Plan adoption at risk with only £1m contingency for delivery against planning reform uncertainty
findings.detail: The council lacks an up-to-date Local Plan and 'only has a low level of housing supply', creating vulnerability to speculative applications 'more difficult to resist'. The budget provides £1m contingency for 2026-27 (with £2m approved in March 2025 for evidence work). Delivery is at risk given ongoing central planning reform and Green Belt designation pressure (70% of borough previously Green Belt).
findings.matters: Failure to adopt a Local Plan leaves the council exposed to developer pressure and uncontrolled growth costs. The contingency provision may prove insufficient if reform accelerates.
findings.figures: £2m approved March 2025 for Local Plan evidence and master planning; £1m contingency 2026-27; 70% of borough previously Green Belt
findings.quote: The Council does not currently have an up-to-date Local Plan and only has a low level of housing supply, and therefore is at risk of speculative applications for development, which are more difficult to resist.

findings.headline: Core Spending Power now includes business rates growth previously treated as uncertain one-off funding
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review now embeds retained business rates growth (£0 indicated for 2026-27, but previously £3.6-4.5m) into Core Spending Power. The council has a long-standing policy of treating this as one-off due to 'uncertain future and the pending Business Rates baseline reset'. The budget required emergency 'Adjustment Support Grant' (£255k) after the provisional settlement changed business rates pooling allocation.
findings.matters: If business rates growth does not materialise or the baseline resets unfavourably, the council has already committed this funding to service delivery and cannot easily reverse without a deficit.
findings.figures: CSP base year 2025-26 reallocated 50:50 to counties (from 100% to districts); £255k adjustment support grant required to protect provisional position; pooling gains historically volatile
findings.quote: the Council should consider how to apply it revised CSP in relation to supporting frontline services whilst also maintaining the financial discipline for funding one off spend and minimising the financial impact of capital financing on the revenue budget.

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention difficulties forcing higher pay settlements, masking service risk
findings.detail: The CFO identifies recruitment and retention as a 'key concern' creating service pressures that 'could significantly impact service provision going forward if not properly addressed'. Staff consultation showed 74% opposed the proposed 3% pay award, forcing Cabinet to approve 4% (£828k). Personnel Committee cited 'high cost of agency staff' and concerns that 2025-26 award (3%) fell behind the NJC award (3.2%).
findings.matters: Forced pay increases above government assumptions, driven by retention pressure, are revenue-consuming and may not resolve underlying service capacity issues.
findings.figures: Pay award 4.0% (£828k) versus proposed 3%; 74% of staff survey opposed 3% offer; Hertsmere 2025-26 (3%) behind NJC (3.2%)
findings.quote: In some areas recruitment and retention continues to cause service pressures and could significantly impact service provision going forward if not properly addressed.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand doubled in five years, creating ongoing subsidy requirement
findings.detail: Homelessness approaches have doubled from 822 (2019-20) to 1,652 (2024-25). Prevention work has constrained temporary accommodation numbers but placement costs remain 'well in excess of the level of Housing Benefit residents can claim'. The council now funds an additional £40k annually for Hepburn Court after Hertfordshire County withdrew housing-related support, with private landlord alternatives costing up to £118k per annum.
findings.matters: Doubling demand is an uncontrolled cost pressure that prevention investment has not reversed, and withdrawal of county funding creates new unfunded ongoing obligations.
findings.figures: Homelessness approaches: 822 (2019-20) → 1,652 (2024-25); Hepburn Court support £40k p.a.; alternative provision 'up to £118k per annum'
findings.quote: Homelessness approaches to the Council doubling since 2019/20, when the Council had 822 homelessness approaches compared to 1,652 approaches in 24/25.

findings.headline: Investment income budget of £1.5m at risk as reserves deploy to capital
findings.detail: The budget relies on investment income of £1.5m (held deliberately below the £2.6m estimated return, anticipating reserve drawdown). As the council executes its £40m capital programme, average investment balances are forecast to decline from £68.2m in 2026-27 onwards, causing investment income to 'potentially reduce'. The CFO explicitly notes this income is 'sustainable in the short term' only.
findings.matters: Investment income (£1.5m or 8.2% of net budget requirement) is material to the balanced position. Declining balances from capital deployment create an unresolved medium-term revenue gap.
findings.figures: Average investment balance 2026/27: £68.2m; estimated return £2.6m; budget provision £1.5m; £40m capital programme over 4 years
findings.quote: Whilst this income is sustainable in the short term, as the Council continues to invest in its ambitious capital programme, which appears elsewhere on this agenda, the funds available to invest are set to reduce and this income stream will potentially reduce.

findings.headline: Council faces imminent external PWLB borrowing as internal resources exhaust
findings.detail: Hertsmere currently has no external borrowing but acknowledges a Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) of £20.3m, currently covered by internal borrowing (utilising cash balances). The CFO explicitly states 'the need to raise external borrowing moves ever closer'. At current PWLB rates, external borrowing for the unfunded CFR could cost 'in excess of £0.8m' annually.
findings.matters: Shift from internal to external borrowing increases annual revenue costs and lock-in duration risk at a time when reserves are depleting.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £20.3m; borrowing cost 'in excess of £0.8m'; investment income budget held at £1.5m against £2.6m potential return
findings.quote: The Council does not currently have any external borrowing it does however have a need to borrow for capital spend that has not yet been financed. This need to borrow is known as the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) and currently stands at £20.3m.

findings.headline: Reserves forecast to be significantly depleted by 2028-29 due to ambitious capital programme
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly warns reserves will be 'significantly depleted' by 2028-29 as the council executes a £40m capital investment programme and funds one-off costs for Local Plan and Local Government Reorganisation. Useable reserves are falling from £47.7m (April 2025) to £40.6m (March 2026 forecast). The council is drawing down reserves rapidly to fund capital spend.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion eliminates the council's financial resilience and ability to manage revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs, increasing refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £40.6m useable reserves forecast 31 March 2026 (down from £47.7m); £40m capital programme 2025/26-2028/29; reserves expected 'significantly depleted' by 2028/29
findings.quote: by 2028/29, due to the ambitious capital investment as well the one-off costs associated with the Local Plan and Local Government Reorganisation, reserves to be significantly depleted.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 and Prudential Indicators 2025-26 - 2028-29
findings.headline: Investment income significantly exceeds budget, with £3.371m forecast for 2025/26 against revised budget of £1.720m.
findings.detail: 2025/26 investment income is forecast at £3.371m, representing a favorable variance of £1.651m against the revised budget. This favorable outturn compares to 2024/25 when actual investment income was £3,032k against a budget of £1,100k. The high returns reflect both better interest rate environment and substantial liquid cash holdings.
findings.matters: Significant overperformance on investment income suggests strong cash management and liquidity position; however, the large balances also indicate capital spending is not keeping pace with planned deployment.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast: £3.371m (variance +£1.651m); 2024/25 actual: £3,032k vs budget £1,100k
findings.quote: Investment income of £3.371m is forecasted for the year – a favourable variance of £1.651m compared to the revised budget of £1.720m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 and Prudential Indicators 2025-26 - 2028-29
findings.headline: Capital program slippage contributed to higher than planned cash balances of £77.3m.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 outturn report identifies slippage in capital program delivery as a factor contributing to favorable variances and additional cash balances available for investment. The average level of funds available for investment in 2024/25 was £77,268k earning 3.92%. This suggests actual capital spending is trailing planned delivery.
findings.matters: Capital program slippage can indicate either prudent re-forecasting or execution delays; lenders monitor whether capital plans are being delivered as committed and whether cash balances reflect genuinely available liquidity or timing issues.
findings.figures: Average funds available for investment 2024/25: £77,268k at 3.92% average return
findings.quote: This favourable variance was due to stable increase in investment rates over the course of the year, additional investment balances due to additional receipts as well as slippage in the delivery of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 and Prudential Indicators 2025-26 - 2028-29
findings.headline: MRP charge doubled to £490k annually from 2023/24, driven by Platinum Stages project at Elstree Studios.
findings.detail: The council's Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge increased from £240k to £490k per annum in 2023/24. This increase reflects the need to make annual revenue provisions against unfunded capital spend, specifically to fund the Platinum Stages project at Elstree Studios. The Prudential Code requires this MRP policy to be approved annually.
findings.matters: A doubling of MRP provision indicates increased capital financing requirements and shows the council is making prudent annual provision against capital commitments, which affects revenue budget sustainability.
findings.figures: MRP charge £240k per annum (prior), now £490k per annum (from 2023/24)
findings.quote: The total MRP charge from 2023/24 increased to £490k per annum which includes the funding of the Platinum Stages project at Elstree Studios.

findings.headline: No adopted Local Plan since withdrawal in late 2022; accelerated new plan timeline with material risks
findings.detail: The council has no adopted Local Plan following withdrawal of the previous plan in late 2022. An accelerated timeline was approved by Cabinet in March 2025 targeting: stakeholder engagement Feb 2025–Mar 2026, Regulation 18 consultation Jan–Feb 2026, Regulation 19 consultation Apr–May 2026, submission Jun/Jul 2026, and adoption Sep 2027. The council's own risk register identifies several high-risk items: national policy changes (score 12), staff capacity (score 12), financial resources (score 8), and external party deadlines (score 9). The council has committed approximately £2m in additional funding for external consultancy and technical studies.
findings.matters: Without an adopted Local Plan, the council has reduced control over development and is vulnerable to speculative applications and appeals. This contributes to the planning designation risk already identified. Loss of planning control undermines long-term financial planning and creates uncertainty for both the council and investors.
findings.figures: £2m additional funding committed to Local Plan development; submission target June/July 2026; adoption target September 2027
findings.quote: Without a clear planning framework, the council has reduced control over where and how development takes place, making it more vulnerable to speculative applications and appeals. This can lead to uncoordinated growth, pressure on infrastructure, and missed opportunities for sustainable development.

findings.headline: Control deficiencies identified in property valuation assessment and year-end accruals process
findings.detail: Auditors report that design and implementation of management review controls are ineffective in two material areas: (1) the property valuation control relating to PPE valued at £179.8m, and (2) the Council's assessment of year-end accruals. While auditors acknowledge IFRS makes these inherently difficult controls to design, the deficiencies remain. Additionally, there is a flaw in the eFinancials system allowing journals to post without required segregation of duties; auditors identified 1 instance during the year and reiterated a prior-year recommendation on this issue.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in property valuation and accruals increase the risk of material undetected misstatement, particularly given that auditors already cannot fully verify these areas.
findings.figures: Property valued at £179.8m; journal segregation of duties issue: 1 instance identified
findings.quote: The design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area is ineffective in line with the ISA definition. The ISAs acknowledge that it is difficult for management to design controls that address subjectivity and estimation uncertainty in a manner that effectively prevents, or detects and corrects, material misstatements.

findings.headline: Planning Inspectorate designation risk: four of six major appeals allowed in last two years, creating risk of loss of planning fee income and developer contributions
findings.detail: The Planning Inspectorate flagged the council as at risk of designation (where MHCLG takes over major planning decisions) due to poor decision-making quality on major applications. Four of the six major application appeals brought in the last two years have been successful (upheld). Most recently, the Sky Phase 2 appeal was allowed in September 2025. If designated, the council loses planning fee income (Section 62A applications generate zero fees to the council despite the council still performing consultations) and loses Section 106 and other developer contribution commitments. This is identified as a significant value-for-money weakness.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is material to the council's finances and discretionary resources. Loss of this income and discretionary developer contributions would directly impact financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Four of six major application appeals allowed; Planning Inspectorate benchmark is that allowed appeals should not exceed 10% of major applications in a 24-month period
findings.quote: While the Authority avoided being placed in Designation in 2024/25, the recent successful Section 78 appeal in respect of land North of Sky Studios, Elstree (commonly referred to as Sky Phase 2) in September 2025, in addition to the fact that four of the six major application appeals brought in the last two years have now been successful, significantly increases the likelihood that the Council will enter Designation by the Planning Inspectorate in the coming months.

findings.headline: Financial reporting deadlines missed: draft accounts published 25 July 2025, after statutory 30 June deadline
findings.detail: The council failed to meet its statutory obligation to publish draft accounts by 31 May (they published 25 July). This is identified as a significant value-for-money weakness in governance. The root causes were delays in prior year audit completion (2022/23, 2023/24), departure of the Senior Finance Accountant at year-end, two unsuccessful recruitment rounds, and broader finance team capacity pressures. Management response indicates a new finance officer is joining December 2025 and the timetable will be reviewed to align with statutory deadlines.
findings.matters: Persistent inability to meet statutory deadlines signals weak financial controls and governance, and indicates underlying capacity problems in the finance function that may affect the reliability of the accounting system.
findings.figures: Draft accounts published 25 July 2025 (deadline was 30 June 2025 or 31 May depending on regulation); prior year also delayed with disclaimed opinion issued 28 February 2025
findings.quote: The Council's unaudited, draft accounts for 2024/25 were published on the Council's website on 25 July 2025, therefore failing to meet the requirement to publish draft annual Statement of Accounts by 30 June.

findings.headline: Auditors cannot verify the financial statements and issue a disclaimer of opinion instead of a clean audit opinion
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. The areas they cannot verify include cash, property and equipment (£179.8m), debtors, creditors, pension scheme assets, impairments, business rates provisions, and the movement in reserves between usable and unusable categories. Any adjustments would have consequential effects on net assets, reserve classification, collection fund and income/expenditure. This is a continuation from the 2023/24 audit which also had a disclaimer.
findings.matters: A lender cannot verify the council's actual financial position, reserve adequacy, or liquidity when the auditor disclaims an opinion. This is the most fundamental governance failure.
findings.figures: Property and equipment valued at £179.8m (2025) and £177.3m (2024); total usable reserves £47.7m; cash position £34.7m
findings.quote: We have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over a number of areas of the financial statements as we have been unable to perform the procedures that we consider necessary to form our opinion on the financial statements ahead of the Backstop Date. These areas include, but were not limited to: Cash, Property, Plant and Equipment, Short-Term and Long-Term Debtors, Short-Term and Long-Term Creditors, and the Fair Value of Scheme Assets

findings.paper_title: 20260129A-A2628- Risk focus report - SO31 and SO51-Planning
findings.headline: Special Measures designation would eliminate planning fee income and S106 negotiation
findings.detail: Explicit consequences of designation include loss of planning fee income and inability to negotiate S106 agreements—both material funding sources. The council would also incur opportunity costs managing applications without payment, with no income offset mentioned.
findings.matters: Planning fees and S106 contributions are direct revenue sources; loss of both would materially impact the council's financial position—a risk to resilience that a lender would monitor closely.
findings.figures: Planning fee income and S106 negotiation ability identified as consequences of designation with no mitigation or replacement funding sources mentioned
findings.quote: The consequence of being designated as a special measures planning authority include: loss of planning fee income. inability to negotiate S106 agreements. Opportunity costs of managing the administration element of these applications without payment.

findings.paper_title: 20260129A-A2628- Risk focus report - SO31 and SO51-Planning
findings.headline: Council rated 'Very Likely' to be designated a Special Measures Planning Authority
findings.detail: The council faces designation as a Special Measures Planning Authority due to a high percentage of planning decisions being overturned at appeal; the threshold for triggering designation has recently been reduced. This carries the 'highest impact and likelihood' in the council's risk framework. Once designated, certain planning applications bypass council scrutiny and must be submitted directly to the Planning Inspectorate.
findings.matters: This designation removes the council's planning discretion—a governance failure that signals planning decision-making problems or inadequate resourcing in the planning function.
findings.figures: 'Very Likely' probability with 'highest impact and likelihood' in risk framework; triggered by high appeal overturn rate with threshold recently reduced
findings.quote: This risk has the highest impact and likelihood in the risk management framework. The likelihood is rated as "Very Likely" in view of the high percentage of planning decisions being overturned at appeal and the reduction in the threshold percentage.

findings.headline: Hertsmere Development Limited winding up with financial position not disclosed in public forum.
findings.detail: The council's property development company, Hertsmere Development Limited (HDL), has no further projects in the pipeline and is being wound up. The Assistant Director of Finance, who is a director of the company, declined to discuss its financial position in the public committee meeting, offering only to discuss it with the Chair separately.
findings.matters: A development company being wound down could be carrying financial losses or liabilities that are not being disclosed in the public financial strategy. The refusal to discuss finances publicly creates uncertainty about whether there are contingent liabilities or financial consequences of the wind-up that creditors should be aware of.
findings.figures: No financial figures disclosed
findings.quote: Hertsmere Development Limited (HDL) has no further projects in the pipeline, so it looked likely it would be wound up. He said it would not be appropriate to discuss the company's finances in a public forum.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows balanced position over 2026/27 to 2028/29 following Fair Funding Review settlement.
findings.detail: The updated Medium Term Financial Plan incorporates the multi-year financial settlement announced on 17 December 2025 and demonstrates that the council can balance its revenue budget across the three-year planning period. This represents the council's response to the outcome of the Fair Funding Review.
findings.matters: A demonstrated balanced position across the medium term is essential context for assessing the council's financial stability, though the quality of the balance depends on whether it relies on genuine revenue-expenditure alignment or on reserve drawdowns and other one-off measures.
findings.figures: Balanced position demonstrated over 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: The Financial Strategy includes an updated Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) which now takes into account the multi-year financial settlement over the spending review period 2026/27 to 2028/29 and shows balanced position over this period.

findings.headline: Council Tax increase capped at 3% legal maximum, insufficient to keep pace with inflation.
findings.detail: The finance team recommended a 3% Council Tax increase for 2026/27. This represents the legal limit that a district council such as Hertsmere can apply without triggering a local referendum. Even at this maximum level, the increase will not keep pace with inflation, creating a real-terms income decline.
findings.matters: When council tax increases fall short of inflation whilst service costs rise, the council faces a structural income squeeze. This forces either service reductions, deeper efficiency savings, or reliance on reserves or other funding sources to balance budgets.
findings.figures: 3% Council Tax increase recommended; insufficient to keep pace with inflation
findings.quote: The Assistant Director (Finance) said he was recommending a 3% Council Tax increase, but even this increase would not keep pace with inflation. This was the legal limit a Council such as Hertsmere Borough Council could apply without a local referendum.

findings.headline: Homelessness support identified as a multi-year risk area, with funding mechanism changes expected under Fair Funding Review.
findings.detail: The council has identified support for homeless people and homelessness prevention as a risk area for several years. The Fair Funding Review is expected to change the funding mechanism, with the temporary accommodation element separated out as a distinct fund. There is uncertainty about whether overall funding levels will be maintained at current levels.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation are major and volatile cost drivers for councils, often difficult to control or forecast. Uncertainty about future funding levels for a known cost pressure creates budget volatility and the risk of unbudgeted expenditure.
findings.figures: No specific spend figures disclosed
findings.quote: support for homeless people and homeless prevention had been a risk area for several years. The Council had received a Homelessness Prevention Grant, and other additional support, in the preceding year, but the mechanism was likely to change in the Fair Funding Review.

findings.headline: Contingency budget increased by £200k to £500k in response to identified budgetary pressures and uncertainties.
findings.detail: Following Policy Committee comments and to reflect current budgetary pressures, risks and uncertainties, the contingency reserve for 2026/27 has been increased from £300k to £500k. This uplift signals that the finance team anticipates elevated financial volatility in the coming year.
findings.matters: A significant increase in contingency provision is an indicator that the council anticipates financial risks it cannot yet fully quantify or budget for, reflecting diminished confidence in stable expenditure or income forecasting.
findings.figures: Contingency increased to £500k in 2026/27 from £300k in 2025/26; uplift of £200k
findings.quote: the contingency budget for 2026/27 has now been increased to £500k an uplift of £200k from the current 2025/26 contingency budget of £300k

findings.headline: Hertsmere ceases to exist as an entity on 1 April 2028 when Local Government Reorganisation creates new unitary authorities.
findings.detail: The government's Local Government Reorganisation programme will dissolve Hertsmere Borough Council and replace it with a new unitary authority from April 2028. Hertfordshire authorities have submitted joint proposals to government for the restructuring. This creates a hard deadline of 2.5 years within which the council must transition to new governance arrangements.
findings.matters: For lenders, the impending dissolution raises material questions about whether existing borrowing covenants remain valid post-April 2028, who assumes the council's liabilities and bond obligations, and how the reorganisation affects creditworthiness during and after the transition.
findings.figures: April 2028 inception date for new unitary authorities
findings.quote: The Government's timetable for LGR would see inception of the new unitary authorities from April 2028, when Hertsmere would cease to exist as an entity.

news_drafts.headline: Usable capital reserves forecast to decline 84% over three years, from £30.8m to £5.1m
news_drafts.lead: Sharp decline in capital funding capacity constrains ability to fund future capital without increased borrowing or reserves depletion; uncertainty about Dove Lane adds execution risk

news_drafts.headline: Council carries £26.3m of unfunded capital spend funded through internal borrowing against cash balances
news_drafts.lead: Significant internal borrowing constrains future borrowing capacity and ties up cash reserves that could provide liquidity buffer; indicates previous capital decisions created ongoing funding gaps

news_drafts.headline: £2.9m planned development of Cannon Public House cancelled; property now held for sale
news_drafts.lead: Signals a shift in council investment strategy; conversion of development asset to sale removes planned future capital release and suggests development challenges
